topic: Compiler Synthesis of Default Constructors and Member Initialization
explanation: In C++, when a class does not explicitly define a default constructor, the compiler synthesizes one to ensure objects can be default-initialized. This synthesis involves generating code that initializes all non-static data members and base classes in a specific order: first, virtual base classes (if any), then direct base classes, and finally the derived class members. The synthesized default constructor typically calls the default constructors of base classes and member objects, using value initialization for built-ins if they are in a member initialization list or otherwise left uninitialized (though modern standards like C++11+ may zero-initialize them in certain contexts). Implementation-wise, the compiler inserts calls to these constructors at the beginning of the synthesized function, ensuring proper memory layout and alignment. For example, if a class has members of class types, the compiler generates code to invoke their default constructors, which may involve additional vtable setups if those members are polymorphic. Runtime behavior includes stack or heap allocation followed by constructor invocation, with potential padding for alignment (e.g., on x86-64, structs might have 8-byte alignment). Performance implications include slight overhead from synthesized calls, which compilers optimize by inlining where possible, but cross-platform differences exist: GCC might aggressively inline, while MSVC could add debugging hooks. This mechanism ensures the C++ object model maintains invariants like fully constructed objects before use, distinguishing compile-time synthesis from runtime execution.
